description: We want to make learning about space exploration more exciting, interactive, and accessible to everyone. Through immersive experiences and stories rooted in real science, our project brings space missions to life, showing that their impact doesn't end when the mission does. We hope to spark curiosity, inspire young minds, and help people see how every mission contributes to humanity's journey beyond Earth.
summary:
Nobotara71 is a free 3D browser game that lets school-age explorers operate the hardware NASA left behind, instead of reading about it. It answers "Abandoned but not Forgotten" with three narrated missions. Players drive across Tranquility Base to inspect what Apollo 11 left on the Moon, turn Voyager 1's dish back toward Earth from interstellar space, and rebuild the plan to bring Perseverance's sample tubes home from Mars. Each object shows why it was left and what science it made possible. SpaceAI, a guide that answers from NASA pages and lists its sources, takes their follow-up questions.
The missions are famous; the machines they left are not. The name honors the freedom fighters of Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War, in the same belief: no legacy deserves to be forgotten.
details:
The Problem

NASA keeps detailed records of every machine it has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Young people rarely meet them, for three reasons:

  1. Limited awareness: Students hear about active missions and famous milestones, not the hardware that stayed behind.
  2. Barriers to understanding: Technical archives assume knowledge a beginner does not have.
  3. An overlooked legacy: Inactive equipment is treated as debris, so the science it made possible goes untold.

What it does

Nobotara71 turns three pieces of that legacy into missions for students aged 9 to 15 and casual space fans. Each can be played alone, in any order.

The game's Voyager distance is tied to NASA's tracking, and it counts down to 18 November 2026, when Voyager 1 becomes the first spacecraft one light-day from Earth.

What makes it different

Platforms such as NASA Eyes, SpaceEngine and Universe Sandbox let people view or simulate space. Nobotara71 takes a different editorial approach: it tells the story of what missions left behind, and has the player operate it.

  1. Left-behind hardware is the subject. The missions are famous. The descent stage, the reflector and the sample tubes are not.
  2. Heritage, not debris. Each object is shown still doing a job or still holding a question
  3. Unfinished ambitions. The original Mars Sample Return plan never flew, yet it left evidence, a method and a question worth going back for.
  4. A Bangladesh-inspired perspective. The spirit of remembrance and perseverance from the 1971 Liberation War connects historical memory with preserving humanity's technological legacy.

Our guiding philosophy: "No legacy deserves to be forgotten."

How it works

  1. Choose a mission; The home page opens on a title screen with the three missions.
  2. Enter the 3D world; Each mission loads its own environment in the browser, with nothing to install.
  3. Explore; Players use the keyboard or on-screen controls, follow one active marker, and interact with each object.
  4. Operate, don't read; Every mission has objectives, inspections and a puzzle built on a real engineering trade-off.
  5. Listen; Every line is narrated and shown as text. The voices are AI-generated and labelled AI VOICE on screen.
  6. Ask SpaceAI. The guide retrieves passages from indexed NASA pages, answers in simple words, and lists the pages it used. When those pages do not cover a question, it says the answer comes from general knowledge.
  7. Finish. A closing scene sums up what the hardware left behind. Played in order, Apollo 11 leads to Voyager 1, then to Mars.

Fiction is marked as fiction. Voyager's "last transmission" carries a disclaimer, and the question of life on Mars is left open.

Benefits

  • Understanding. Technical records become stories with one idea at a time
  • Learning by doing. Students find out why a descent stage was built not to return by handling the trade-off themselves.
  • Trust. Facts come from NASA's published results, and SpaceAI shows its sources
  • Access. It is free, needs no login, runs on laptops and phones, and every spoken line has text
  • A wider perspective. The Bangladesh 1971 tribute ties remembering space heritage to remembering human courage.

Primary application

Nobotara71 can serve as a supplementary learning resource in schools, colleges and science clubs. A teacher can introduce Apollo 11, Voyager 1 or Mars Sample Return with one mission, then let students investigate their own questions with SpaceAI.

The project has not yet been formally tested with students. That is the first step of our plan.

What we hope to achieve

Our vision is that discarded space hardware is seen as lasting scientific heritage, not forgotten debris. We set three objectives, each with a way to measure it:

Roadmap (12 months)

  1. Prototype stabilisation, months 1 to 3: Fix known issues, re-verify every fact against NASA sources, improve SpaceAI's source attribution, and test on common desktop and mobile browsers.
  2. User testing, months 4 to 6. Run structured sessions with students, collect feedback from teachers, and publish the findings.
  3. Mission expansion, months 7 to 9. Add missions from NASA's list of left-behind hardware, such as the Mars rovers and the Pioneer probes, and extend SpaceAI's sources to cover them.
  4. Platform development, months 10 to 12. Add learning materials for each mission and pilot the platform in schools, colleges and science clubs.

Long-term, we want Nobotara71 to become an interactive archive of the hardware humanity has left across the solar system.

Tools, languages and software

NASA Data

Nobotara71 uses NASA 3D models, NASA photographs, and facts and figures from NASA's published results. It does not use live data feeds or raw datasets. The challenge's own resource list (Apollo Lunar Module descent stages, retroreflectors, deep-space probes) shaped which hardware we chose

Models and images

  1.  Mars 2020 Perseverance rover model, NASA 3D Resources (credit NASA/JPL): Reduced in Blender
  2. and driven by the player in Mission 03
  3. NASA Mars globe, NASA 3D Resources (credit NASA/JPL): Opening and final shots of Mission 03
  4. Voyager model: The spacecraft the player turns in Mission 02
  5. Apollo Lunar Module descent stage model: Eagle's descent stage in Mission 01
  6. Earth model with Blue Marble imagery: Earth in the lunar sky in Mission 01
  7. Apollo 11 plaque photograph: Shown when the player inspects the plaque
  8. Voyager Golden Record cover photograph: Shown in the Golden Record pages

Facts and figures

  1. NASA/JPL Horizons
    What we took from it: Voyager 1's distance from Earth (25,880,381,236 km on 9 November 2026) and its direction of travel
    Where it appears: Mission 02 distance, light-time and the one light-day countdown
  2. NASA and JPL Voyager mission pages, including the April 2026 instrument shutdown
    What we took from it: The 2012 heliopause crossing, plasma density, magnetic field and particle results, power loss of about 4 W a year, Golden Record contents
    Where it appears: Mission 02 readings, power trade-off and archive quiz
  3. NSSDCA Master Catalog and the Apollo 11 Mission Report
    What we took from it: Landing time and site, time on the surface, sample mass, what the descent stage, retroreflector and plaque are
    Where it appears: Mission 01 objects and facts, SpaceAI
  4. NASA Mars 2020 mission pages
    What we took from it: Jezero Crater's lake and delta, rock types, the ten-tube depot at Three Forks, the Cheyava Falls rock, the Mars Sample Return plan
    Where it appears: Mission 03 scans, clues and the return-plan puzzle

SpaceAI answers from an index of NASA web pages on these three missions and lists the pages it used under each answer.

Space Agency Partner & Other Data

Space agency partner

  • European Space Agency (ESA): Mars Sample Return was a joint NASA and ESA plan. Mission 03 describes ESA's Earth Return Orbiter as one of its five steps.

Our own work

  • The lunar terrain, the laser retroreflector model, the Sun, and the Mars crater, rocks, sample tubes and holograms (made in Blender or built in code)
  • All mission scripts, puzzles, interface design and sound effects (synthesised with the Web Audio API)

Open-source software and services

  • React, Three.js and its Draco decoder, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Motion, Lucide, react-markdown, Express (local development only), TypeScript.
  • Blender and FFmpeg for assets and audio.
  • Google Gemini API, Cloudflare Pages and Workers
  • Typefaces: Plus Jakarta Sans and Space Mono (Google Fonts)

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes, we used SI tools. SI does not drive the gameplay, decide puzzle answers or generate the missions.

The team directed, reviewed and tested all AI-assisted code.

Neil Armstrong's voice in Mission 01 is an AI portrayal. The words were written for the game and are not quotations. The panel shows "Neil Armstrong (Portrayed)" and AI VOICE.

No AI-generated content uses or modifies NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
